name: AI for Productivity and Leadership
objectives: Given a list of a team's tasks for the week, use an AI assistant to build a prioritized weekly plan with an owner for each task, and correct anything it got wrong using your own judgment
Given a messy note to a manager, write a bottom-line-up-front (BLUF) email with AI help, with the main point in the first sentence and a friendly, professional tone
Given a short set of meeting notes, turn the notes into decisions, action items and open questions with AI, with one owner and a due date on every action item
Given something a teammate did, draft feedback in situation-behavior-impact form and rewrite it in your own words, describing only behavior you saw
Given a task you could hand off, create a delegation checklist with purpose, standard, deadline, resources and check-ins, with every required part

Whenever you use AI with team or company information, follow your employer's AI policy, use roles instead of names and keep private information out, with no private details in any prompt and you responsible for the final work

lessons.title: Lesson 1: From mission planning to a weekly team plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to turn a list of tasks into a prioritized weekly plan with owners.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of a team's tasks for the week, you will use an AI assistant to build a prioritized weekly plan with an owner for each task, and correct anything it got wrong using your own judgment.
In the military you planned from the mission: what must get done, by when, with what people and resources. Civilian teams need the same thing; they often call it a work plan or project plan.
Give an AI assistant your list of tasks, deadlines and team roles, and ask it to sort them by priority and lay out the week. Example: "Here are 8 tasks for my 5-person warehouse team this week, with deadlines. Sort them by urgency and importance and make a Monday-to-Friday table with an owner role for each."
Use roles, not full names ("Shift lead A", "Forklift operator 2"). Then apply your judgment: AI does not know that one person is on leave or that one customer matters most. You adjust and approve the plan.
Step by step:
- List the week's tasks and deadlines.
- List team roles, not names.
- Ask AI to sort by urgency and importance and make a weekly table.
- Adjust for what AI does not know: leave, skills, key customers.
- Share the final plan with the team.
Words to know:
- Work plan: a list of tasks with owners and dates; the civilian version of an operations plan.
- Urgent vs important: urgent needs action now; important matters most to the goal. Not always the same.
Try it now: Write six tasks your team (real or practice) must do this week. Ask an AI assistant to sort them by urgency and importance and lay out a Monday-to-Friday table with an owner role for each. Change one thing it got wrong.
You can now turn a list of tasks into a prioritized weekly team plan with AI, and correct it with your judgment.

check.q: What does it mean to sort tasks by urgency and importance?
options: Do the easiest tasks first
Decide which tasks need doing soon and which matter most
Give every task to one person
Do tasks in alphabetical order
check.why: Urgent and important are different, so sorting by both shows what to do first.

check.q: The AI's weekly plan gives all six tasks to the same person. What do you do?
options: Accept it because the AI decided
Delete the plan and do it all yourself
Ask the AI to add more tasks
Use your judgment to spread the work and fix the plan
check.why: The AI drafts the plan, but you know your team and approve the final version.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing BLUF emails and updates
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short bottom-line-up-front email with AI help.
This lesson builds toward: Given a messy note to a manager, you will write a bottom-line-up-front (BLUF) email with AI help, with the main point in the first sentence and a friendly, professional tone.
BLUF, bottom line up front, works in civilian offices too, even if people do not use the term. Put the main point or the decision you need in the first sentence. Then give the short reasons and the next steps.
Ask the AI to rewrite a long draft: "Rewrite this as a short email to my manager. Put the bottom line in the first sentence, then three bullet points, then the next step. Friendly, professional tone. No military terms."
Check the tone. Military writing can sound blunt to civilian readers. A simple "Thanks" or "Happy to discuss" helps. Read it once as the person receiving it.
Step by step:
- Write what you need to say, even if messy.
- Ask AI to put the bottom line first, then bullets, then the next step.
- Ask it to remove military terms and use a friendly, professional tone.
- Read it as the receiver and fix anything unclear.
Words to know:
- BLUF: bottom line up front: the main point or request goes first.
- Tone: how your writing sounds to the reader: friendly, blunt, formal.
Try it now: Write a messy note to a manager about a delay on a task. Ask an AI assistant to rewrite it as a BLUF email with three bullets and a next step, in a friendly, professional tone.
You can now write a short, clear bottom-line-up-front email that suits a civilian workplace.

check.q: In a BLUF email, what comes first?
options: The main point or request
A long background story
Your signature
A list of everyone who helped
check.why: Bottom line up front means the reader sees the key point or request right away.

check.q: Your AI-drafted email sounds short and blunt. What do you do before sending?
options: Send it as it is
Make it twice as long
Add a friendly line and read it as the receiver would
Remove the main point
check.why: A friendly line and a read-through as the receiver keep it clear and professional.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Turning meeting notes into action items
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to turn meeting notes into an action-item table with owners and due dates.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short set of meeting notes, you will turn the notes into decisions, action items and open questions with AI, with one owner and a due date on every action item.
Meetings waste time when nobody leaves knowing who does what. An after-action habit fixes that: what was decided, who owns each action, and when it is due.
Paste your notes (with roles instead of names, and no private details) and ask: "Turn these notes into: 1) decisions made, 2) a table of action items with owner and due date, 3) open questions." If an action has no owner or date, the AI should flag it.
Many workplace tools, such as Microsoft Teams with Copilot or Google Meet with Gemini, can summarize meetings if your employer has turned that on. Follow your employer's rules about recording and AI, and tell people when a meeting is being recorded or summarized.
Step by step:
- Take short notes during the meeting.
- Replace names with roles and remove private details.
- Ask AI for decisions, an action table with owner and due date, and open questions.
- Fill in any missing owners or dates.
- Send the summary to the team the same day.
Words to know:
- Action item: a task from a meeting with one owner and a due date.
- After-action review: a short look back: what happened, what worked, what to change.
Try it now: Write five lines of practice meeting notes. Ask an AI assistant to turn them into decisions, an action-item table with owner role and due date, and open questions.
You can now turn meeting notes into a clear action-item table with owners and dates.

check.q: What is an open question in a meeting summary?
options: A task with an owner
A decision the team made
A question nobody may ask
Something still undecided that needs an answer later
check.why: Open questions are issues the meeting did not settle, listed so they are not forgotten.

check.q: The AI's action-item table has "Order parts" with no owner. What do you do?
options: Leave it; someone will do it
Give it one owner and a due date
Give it to everyone
Delete it
check.why: An action item is only complete with one owner and a due date.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Leading people with AI as your aide

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Preparing clear, fair feedback
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft feedback in situation-behavior-impact form, then make it your own.
This lesson builds toward: Given something a teammate did, you will draft feedback in situation-behavior-impact form and rewrite it in your own words, describing only behavior you saw.
Good feedback is specific and about behavior, not personality. A simple model is situation, behavior, impact (SBI): "In Tuesday's shift handoff (situation), you walked through every open order (behavior), and the next shift started with no delays (impact)." It works for praise and for correction.
AI can help you prepare: "Help me write SBI feedback for a team member who has been late to the morning huddle three times this month. Keep it respectful and end with a question that invites their side." Use a role, not a name.
Deliver it yourself, in person or by call, and listen. AI helps you prepare the words; trust between you and your people comes from you.
Step by step:
- Pick one specific situation.
- Describe the behavior you saw, not the person's character.
- Say the impact on the team or the work.
- Ask AI to help phrase it respectfully, using a role not a name.
- Deliver it yourself and listen.
Words to know:
- SBI: situation, behavior, impact: a simple way to give clear feedback.
- Behavior: what someone did or said, which you can see or hear.
Try it now: Think of one thing a teammate did well recently. Ask an AI assistant to help you write SBI praise for it, using a role not a name. Then rewrite it in your own words.
You can now prepare clear, fair situation-behavior-impact feedback with AI help and deliver it yourself.

check.q: In SBI feedback, what is the behavior part?
options: Your opinion of the person's attitude
The date of the meeting
What the person did that you saw or heard
The impact on your mood
check.why: Behavior is the specific action you observed, not a judgment about the person.

check.q: The AI drafted praise for a teammate that sounds stiff. What do you do?
options: Rewrite it in your own words and give it yourself
Email the AI text as it is
Have the AI send it
Skip the praise
check.why: AI can help you prepare, but feedback should be in your words and come from you.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Delegating with a clear checklist
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to build a delegation checklist that states the task, standard, deadline and check-in.
This lesson builds toward: Given a task you could hand off, you will create a delegation checklist with purpose, standard, deadline, resources and check-ins, with every required part.
You know commander's intent: tell people the purpose and the end state, not only the steps, so they can adapt. Civilian delegation works the same way.
A good handoff covers: the task, why it matters (intent), what done looks like (the standard), the deadline, the resources and authority they have, and when you will check in. Ask AI: "Make a one-page delegation checklist for handing off the weekly inventory report to a new team member. Include purpose, standard, deadline, resources and check-in points."
Then hand it off in person, ask them to explain it back, and step back. Check in at the agreed points instead of hovering.
Step by step:
- Name the task and why it matters.
- Describe what done looks like.
- Set the deadline, resources and authority.
- Ask AI to turn this into a one-page checklist.
- Hand it off, ask them to explain it back, and check in as agreed.
Words to know:
- Delegate: give someone else a task and the authority to do it.
- Intent: the purpose and end state of a task, so people can adapt when things change.
Try it now: Pick one task you could hand off. Ask an AI assistant to make a one-page delegation checklist with purpose, standard, deadline, resources and check-in points.
You can now delegate a task with a clear checklist that gives purpose, standard, deadline and check-ins.

check.q: Why include the purpose when you delegate a task?
options: So the person cannot change anything
So the person can adapt if things change
So you never need to check in
So the task takes longer
check.why: Knowing the purpose and end state lets people make good choices when plans change.

check.q: You handed off a report due Friday. What do you do next?
options: Wait until Friday and hope
Take the task back right away
Redo it yourself without asking
Check in at the agreed points
check.why: Agreed check-ins let you catch problems early without micromanaging.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Using AI responsibly as a leader
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use three rules for using AI responsibly with team and company information.
This lesson builds toward: Whenever you use AI with team or company information, you will follow your employer's AI policy, use roles instead of names and keep private information out, with no private details in any prompt and you responsible for the final work.
As a leader you set the example. Rule 1: follow your employer's AI policy. Many companies say which AI tools are approved and what information may go into them. If there is no policy, ask.
Rule 2: keep people's private information out of public AI tools: performance problems by name, health, pay, home addresses, or anything said in confidence. Keep customer and company secrets out too. Use roles and general descriptions.
Rule 3: you own the result. Check facts, numbers and tone before anything goes out. If AI helped write something important, read every word. Telling your team how you use AI, and how they may use it, builds trust.
Step by step:
- Find and read your employer's AI policy, or ask your manager.
- Use only approved tools for work information.
- Keep private and confidential information out of public AI.
- Check everything AI writes before it goes out.
- Tell your team how AI may be used.
Words to know:
- AI policy: an employer's rules about which AI tools may be used and what information may go into them.
- Confidential: information meant to be kept private within a group or company.
Try it now: Final task: for a team of three to six people, use an AI assistant to build a one-week plan with owners, write a BLUF update email, and turn short meeting notes into an action-item table. Use roles instead of names and check that no private information is in any of it.
You can now use AI as a leader in a way that follows policy, protects your people and keeps you accountable.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Weekly plan Tasks are not in priority order, or some have no owner. A one-week plan with priorities and an owner role for each task. The learner changed something the AI got wrong and can say why. BLUF update email The main point is buried, or the tone is blunt. The first sentence states the main point, with short bullets and a next step in a professional tone. The email was read as the receiver would and tightened to the fewest words. Action items Some action items have no owner or no due date. Decisions, action items with one owner and a due date each, and open questions. Due dates fit the weekly plan, and open questions have a person to answer them. Privacy and policy A name or private detail appears in a prompt or the work. Roles instead of names, and no private information anywhere. The learner names the employer's AI policy or the question they would ask their manager about it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which rule comes first when you use AI at work?
options: Follow your employer's AI policy
Use any tool you like
Paste in everything so the AI has context
Let the AI make the final decision
check.why: Your employer's policy decides which tools and information you may use.

check.q: You want AI help with a note about a team member's pay problem. What do you do?
options: Paste in their name and pay details
Paste their whole file
Leave the private details out and describe the situation with a role
Post it in a public chat
check.why: Pay and personal details never go into a public AI tool; a role keeps the person private.
